edges.effect_quant: In older adults, more intensive blood-pressure lowering improves cardiovascular outcomes but increases some hemodynamic adverse events, creating a narrow therapeutic window rather than a simple fall-prevention story. In SPRINT, intensive treatment lowered major cardiovascular events and mortality but caused more serious hypotension and syncope, though not more injurious falls. A meta-analysis limited to adults aged 60 and older similarly concluded that lower targets did not increase falls overall, even while hypotension and syncope were more frequent with aggressive treatment.
edges.population: older adults with hypertension, especially community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older at elevated cardiovascular risk
edges.mechanism: Lowering blood pressure more aggressively can reduce stroke and vascular injury but can also narrow cerebral and systemic perfusion reserve in susceptible older adults. That tradeoff means modest lowering may improve outcomes, whereas overly aggressive lowering can provoke hypotension, syncope, and treatment burden without clearly increasing injurious falls across trials.
edges.summary: The best interpretation is a benefit-harm curve rather than a uniformly helpful or harmful effect on falls. Intensive treatment in selected older adults appears cardiovascularly beneficial and does not clearly raise injurious-fall risk, but it does raise hypotension and syncope risk enough that the ideal target likely depends on frailty, reserve, and time-to-benefit considerations.
edges.caveats: Trial populations such as SPRINT excluded some of the frailest or most orthostatic patients, so real-world fall risk may be less forgiving than the randomized data suggest. This edge should therefore be read as a treatment-window problem in older adults, not as proof that more-intensive control is always either safe or unsafe for mobility outcomes.
